a-payload-written-as-plain-json.text: A payload written as plain JSON.
Ticket #719. Read the plan for the slices, the gate and the files, and the data model, modules model and functions model for the shapes. Base: main at 14d50c40 (release 0.14.0).

story.text: As a reader who has a registry and a key, I store the document {"answer": 42} under the key by writing that file and nothing else. I read the key back and the page shows {"answer": 42}. I did not learn how Plutus data is written in JSON first.
As an integrator who needs exact control of the bytes on chain, I keep writing the detailed schema ({"constructor":0,"fields":[{"int":42}]}) and say so on the command, so nothing is guessed.
As someone with a script from the previous release, my payload file in the detailed schema is refused with a sentence that tells me to say so, never stored as something else.

the-plain-mapping.text: Reading a file in the plain schema turns its JSON into Plutus data by this table, and nothing else. A reader can apply it by hand.
Whole documents are accepted, not only objects: the file may hold 42, "alice" or [1, 2].

Worked by hand: the file {"answer": 42} holds one object with one key, so the data is a map with one entry, the byte string of the text answer (hex 616e73776572) to the integer 42. In the detailed schema that is {"map":[{"k":{"bytes":"616e73776572"},"v":{"int":42}}]}. The file 42 is the integer 42, the same data as the detailed {"int":42}.

reading-the-data-back.text: A stored payload has a plain reading when it is one that this table could have produced: an integer of at most 1000 digits; a byte string that is valid UTF-8, read as text; a list whose items all have a plain reading; a map whose keys are valid UTF-8 byte strings in strictly ascending order of bytes and whose values all have a plain reading; the constructor with index 0 or 1 and no fields, read as false or true. The plain reading is the JSON the table started from. Anything else has none: a byte string that is not text, a map with a key that is not text or keys out of order, any other constructor, a number past the digit limit.
The reading is a property of the data, not of how it was stored. The detailed {"int":42} and the plain 42 store the same data, so both read back as 42.

refusals.text: A refusal names the file, says what it asked for, and names the value and where it is, written as a path from the document: $ is the whole document, .name an object key, [2] an item.

The detailed-schema refusal covers the whole document only. A detailed-looking object nested inside a larger document is plain JSON like any other. Every file the previous release accepted is therefore either refused with the instruction or read exactly as before when the setting is detailed; none is stored as a different datum.
All refusals come before the node is read, so a preview with an unreachable node shows them.

selecting-the-schema.text: The setting is --payload-schema with the values plain and detailed; plain when it is absent. It is not a standing setting: no environment variable, no configuration key. Every command that reads a payload file takes it and reads the file one way:
open-datum insert and open-datum update, with and without --preview;
the insert and update of the negative host, which share the open-datum parser.
No command reads a payload file by any other path.

what-inspect-and-the-update-receipt-prin.text: What inspect and the update receipt print.

open-datum inspect prints the key's payload under payload in the application output, with a field payloadSchema beside it. When the stored data has a plain reading, payload is that JSON and payloadSchema is plain. Otherwise payload is the detailed schema of the data and payloadSchema is detailed. The update receipt prints payload and payloadSchema the same way. The envelope, with the control and the payload in the detailed schema, is printed as before and is the way to read the exact data.
keri-stub status prints its payload the same way, because it runs the same shared inspect code.

what-does-not-change.text: The detailed schema: the same documents are accepted, with the same meanings and the same refusals.

The validators and the script hashes. The open-datum validator reads no payload; the Lean model states that a payload update leaves the registry unchanged and treats the payload as opaque data. Nothing in lean/ or onchain/ is touched.
Data already on chain, and the envelope, the control, the deposit and every transaction the commands build.

observable-acceptance.text: Each line is an invariant with a name and fails when the behaviour is absent.

limits.text: null is not stored. A later release may accept it without changing what is stored today.
The text of a number is not kept: 1.0 is read back as 1.
An object's key order in the file is not kept; stored order is ascending by key bytes. JSON readers do not preserve it and a map in Plutus data is ordered.
A payload with a byte string that is not text, a map with non-text keys or any constructor other than the two booleans needs the detailed schema; it prints in the detailed schema.
A text stored as bytes by the detailed schema reads back as text when the bytes are valid UTF-8; nobody can tell from the chain which form wrote it.

A whole payload that looks like a detailed document, such as {"int": 5} as a plain object, cannot be written in the plain schema because of the refusal above. It can be stored through the detailed schema as a map with the text key; it then reads back as plain JSON, and writing that JSON again needs the detailed form.
The tutorial in the singular-demo repository changes with the release that contains this; its lines are listed in a handoff for the desk. Nothing is pushed there.
